html:
A long burst of growth in Japanese farming in the 1600s, under the peace of Tokugawa Japan. With little foreign trade, Japan fed a population that rose to around 30 million by about 1700, roughly double what it had been a century before.

The end of the civil wars freed men and money for work on the land. Lords and merchants paid to drain marshes, reclaim tidal flats and dig canals and ponds, opening large areas of new rice paddy. Farmers adopted better tools, such as stronger hoes and a toothed comb for threshing rice, and better seed.

Fertiliser was key. Besides night soil from the cities, farmers bought dried sardines and oil cakes, a sign of a growing market economy. Farm manuals spread the best methods; the best known, Nōgyō zensho, appeared in 1697.

Growth slowed after 1700 as the land filled up. Later bad years brought hunger, as in the Tenmei famine of the 1780s. Rice from these fields was traded at the Dōjima Rice Exchange in Osaka.
